title: "J x K Design Allowing Simple Effects Inferences"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{J-K-Design_inference-on-simple-effects}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

A vignette to demonstrate how to conduct either a planned or post-hoc analysis of simple effects contrasts in a J x K design. Simple effects contrasts allow a researcher to analyse cell mean differences at one level of a factor by the level (or levels) of the other factor. This is relevant when trying to understand what may be driving an interaction effect, as an interaction effect contrast may be partitioned into two simple effects contrasts.

In partitioning analysis out at the individual level of a factor, a simple effects analysis produces non-orthogonal families which are incompatible with how an ANOVA F Simultaneous Test Procedure controls the FWER. Instead, and as will be demonstrated in this vignette, a simple effects analysis may define two families - the A and B Simple Effects Families - which allows one to examine either (but not both) A or B simple effects. Alternatively, and at the cost of power, one may define a single non-standard all-factorial contrasts family, allowing for investigation of simple effects, main effects and interaction effects across all families. As such, the FWER is indirectly controlled by directly controlling the Per-Experiment Error Rate at $m$ · ⍺, where $m$ is equal to the number of non-standard families defined.

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

## The Packages

To use PsyR to calculate confidence intervals over contrast effects, we will utilise a workflow with functions from [afex](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/afex/versions/1.4-1) to implement ANOVA models, and [emmeans](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/) to obtain estimated marginal means and the required contrast estimates. So let's load those packages, and any others that are helpful for our workflow.

```{r, loadpackages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(afex)
library(emmeans)
library(PsyR)
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Data

The `experience` dataframe contains the results of a between-subjects experiment examining the interaction between years of experience held by a therapist (10, 3, or less than 1) and type of therapy (Behavioural, Cognitive, Psychotherapy and Group). Behavioural and Cognitive therapies may be described as Directive therapies, whereas Psychotherapy and Group therapy may be described as Talking therapies. A higher score on the dependent variable (outcome of therapy) is indicative of improved mental health.

Let's load the data, then call the `head()` function to print the first 5 rows.

```{r loaddata}
data(experience)
head(experience, 5)
```

To learn more about the `experience` dataframe call the help function using `?df` to open its documentation.

```{r, whatexperience, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
?experience
```

Also, let's tidy up the data, labelling the levels of our independent variables for greater clarity.

```{r sortdata}
experience <- experience %>%
  mutate(
    Experience = factor(
      Experience,
      levels = c("10yrs", "3yrs", "<1yr")
    ),
    Therapy = factor(Therapy,
      levels = c(
        "Behavioural",
        "Cognitive",
        "Psychotherapy",
        "Group"
      )
    )
  )
```

Next, let's visualise our data. Doing so allows us to more intuitively understand its layout.

```{r plotit, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dev = 'svg'}
experience %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = Experience, y = Outcome, colour = Therapy, fill = Therapy, shape = Therapy)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, aes(group = Therapy)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", aes(group = Therapy)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21:24)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```

## The Analysis

Let's prepare to run some statistical tests!

Here we will create the building blocks for first an ANOVA output, and later our Simple Effects Contrasts. To start, let's create the object `mod` by calling the `aov_ez()` function. Of note, defining `mod` in this way will enable emmeans to compute estimated marginal means from which to apply contrasts of interest. Place the `SubjID` column in the ID argument, `Outcome` as our dependent variable, `experience` as our dataframe, and `Experience` and `Therapy` as our between-subjects factors. Finally, create the `emms` object by calling the `emmeans()` function and specifying that we want to take in `mod` (the object we just made) and output according to both `Experience` and `Therapy`. Running this code will give us the cell means for each level of the between-subjects independent variables.

```{r, aov, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
mod <- aov_ez(
  id = "SubjID", 
  dv = "Outcome", 
  data = experience, 
  between = c("Experience", "Therapy")
)

emms <- emmeans(mod, c("Experience", "Therapy"))
knitr::kable(emms, digits = 3)
```

Now let's define and obtain our Factor A (Experience of Therapist) and Factor B (Type of Therapy) contrasts. To do so, create the `experience_contrasts` and `therapy_contrasts` objects, calling `list()` to define our contrasts which compare the following:

**Experience**

- "3yrs - \<1yr" ➞ The difference between therapists with 3 years of experience and therapists with less than 1 year of experience, averaged across types of therapy.

- "10yrs - 3yrs" ➞ The difference between therapists with 10 years of experience and therapists with 3 years of experience, averaged across types of therapy.

**Therapy**

- "Directive - Talking" ➞ The difference between the average of outcomes of Directive therapies (Behavioural and Cognitive) versus the average of Talking therapies (Psychotherapy and Group), averaged across levels of therapist experience.

- "Beh - Cog" ➞ The difference between the average of Behavioural versus Cognitive Therapy, averaged across levels of therapist experience.

- "Psych - Group" ➞ The difference between the average of Psychotherapy versus Group Therapy averaged across levels of therapist experience.

```{r btwn_contrasts}
experience_contrasts = list(
  "3 - <1yr" = c(0, 1, -1),
  "10yrs - 3yrs" = c(1, -1, 0)
)

therapy_contrasts = list(
  "Directive - Talking" = c(0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5),
  "Beh - Cog" = c(1, -1, 0, 0),
  "Psych - Group" = c(0, 0, 1, -1)
)  
```

### Simple Effects

In this analysis, we will define the A [A, A(b)] and interaction (AB) families. This will allow us to understand the impact of experience (Factor A) at the cell levels of each type of therapy (Factor B)

To start, let's calculate the main effects for Factor A. To do so, create `emms_exp` by calling `emmeans()`, placing `mod` in the "Object" argument and the `Experience` column in the "Specs" argument. This code will produce the cell means at each level of Factor A. Next, create `exp_fx` by calling `contrast()`. Place our newly made `emms_exp` in the "Object" argument, `experience_contrasts` in the "Method" argument, and tell the function to make a Bonferroni adjustment. Thus, `exp_fx` will contain the results of a main effects analysis of Factor A (Experience).

```{r, factor_a_fx, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
emms_exp <- emmeans(mod, c("Experience"))
exp_fx <- contrast(emms_exp, experience_contrasts, adjust = "bonferroni")
knitr::kable(exp_fx, digits = 3)
```

Now let's get the A(b) effects: Contrasts of each main effect at the four levels of Factor B (Therapy). To do so, create `Exp_g_therapy` and call `emmeans()`, which will take in a model which attempts to predict our previously made `mod` (which, as a reminder, is an ANOVA table containing simultaneous tests of the main effects of Experience, Therapy, and their interaction) by using scores on Experience holding constant Therapy type. This yields the cell means of each level of Experience at each level of Therapy. Next, to obtain simple effects of the Factor A contrasts at each level of Factor B, create `Ab_fx` and call `contrast()`. Place `Exp_g_therapy` in the "Object" argument, `experience_contrasts` in the "Method" argument, and tell the function to make a Bonferroni adjustment. Thus, the `Ab_fx` object will contain the results of significance tests of our Factor A contrasts (3yrs - \<1yr, and 10yrs - 3yrs) at each level of Therapy.

```{r, A_b, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
Exp_g_therapy <- emmeans(mod, ~ Experience | Therapy)

Ab_fx <- contrast(
  Exp_g_therapy, 
  method = experience_contrasts, 
  adjust = "bonferroni"
)
knitr::kable(Ab_fx, digits = 3)
```

Finally, let's obtain our AB interaction effects. Create `interaction_fx` by calling `contrast()`, placing `emms` in the "Object" argument, and a list containing our previously established Factor A and Factor B contrasts in the "Interaction" argument. Finally, tell the function to make a Bonferroni adjustment.

```{r, AB, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
interaction_fx <- contrast(
  emms,
  interaction = list(experience_contrasts, therapy_contrasts),
  adjust = "bonferroni"
)
knitr::kable(interaction_fx, digits = 3)
```

## Applying PsyR to generate Confidence Intervals

### Planned Analysis with a Bonferonni adjustment

The following section will detail how to conduct an a priori analysis, first of Main and Interaction Effects Contrasts, and second of Simple Effects Contrasts. In doing so, we aim to demonstrate how a Simple Effects analysis can be useful in understanding what is driving interaction effects, as well as how this analysis must be adjusted as compared to an F-STP approach to Main and Interaction Effects.

To run our planned analysis, let's do the following. First, create the object `all_fx` by creating a vector containing lists of the results of significance tests on our Factor A main effects contrasts, A(b) simple effects contrasts, and AB interaction contrasts. Next, create `alphas`, which will take in a list of alphas of equal length to the number of families (2). Here, alpha will be set at $m · ⍺$ ($2 · .05 = .1$).

Next, we will call `psyci()` and input the following.

- The model is set as the previously made `mod` object, where the model must be made using the afex package (and of class afex_aov).

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made `all_fx` list.

- The method is set as "bf" to indicate a Bonferonni adjustment should be enacted.

- Alpha is set at `alphas`, indicating the desired type I error rate should be set per family at .1 (as has been previously established).

- Finally, set independent as `FALSE`. Independent is by default set at `TRUE`, indicating that the correction set in "method" should be applied to each family individually. As we are running a simple effects analysis where we have defined a Factor A family, we need independent to be `FALSE` to appropriately control the type I error rate.

Note that PsyR infers the family and participating factors for every original `emmgrid`, and as such there is no need to specify these features in the `psyci()` function call.

```{r, get_cis_bf}
all_fx <- c(exp_fx, Ab_fx, interaction_fx)
alphas <- rep(list(2 * .05), times = 3)

output_bf <- psyci(
  model = mod, 
  contrast_tables = all_fx, 
  method = "bf", 
  alpha = alphas,
  independent = FALSE
) 

display_bf <- output_bf %>%
  unclass() %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(
    Experience = coalesce(contrast, Experience_custom),
    Therapy = coalesce(Therapy, Therapy_custom),
  ) %>%
  select(estimate:psyr_p_value, Experience, Therapy) %>%
  relocate(Experience, Therapy)

knitr::kable(display_bf, digits = 3)
```

### Post-Hoc Analysis with a Scheffé adjustment

We will now demonstrate how to conduct a post-hoc analysis including A(b) contrasts. Engaging in this method allows one to address contrasts of interest which may emerge after an experiment has taken place, however this comes at the cost of lowered statistical power as compared to an a priori approach. To enact a Scheffé adjustment, conduct the same steps as a planned analysis, with three exceptions. First, "alphas" must be redefined, where $⍺ = 1 - (1 - ⍺)^m$ and $m = 2$ (as there are two standard factorial families contained within the non-standard simple effects family we are analysing). Thus, ⍺ is set at .025 per family. Secondly, we must calculate $ν_1$ and store it within the `nu1` object. Here, $ν_1 = K(J-1)$, so we will run code which captures the number of unique levels of K (Therapy; K = 4) and of J - 1 (Experience; J = 3 ∴ J - 1 = 2). Thus, $ν_1 = 8$. Finally, "method" must be set as post-hoc.

```{r, get_cis_ph}
alphas <- rep(list(1 - (1 - 0.05)^2), times = 3)
nu1 <- length(unique(levels(experience$Therapy))) * 
  (length(unique(levels(experience$Experience))) - 1)

output_ph <- psyci(
  model = mod, 
  contrast_tables = all_fx, 
  method = "ph", 
  alpha = alphas,
  independent = FALSE, 
  nu1 = nu1
) 

display_ph <- output_ph %>%
  unclass() %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(
    Experience = coalesce(contrast, Experience_custom),
    Therapy = coalesce(Therapy, Therapy_custom),
  ) %>%
  select(estimate:psyr_p_value, Experience, Therapy) %>%
  relocate(Experience, Therapy)

knitr::kable(display_ph, digits = 3)
```

### Standard Analysis with Independent Families

Finally, we will demonstrate a standard analysis with independent families of the Main and Interaction Effects. We will do so using a Bonferonni procedure. First, we must calculate the main effects for Factor B: Therapy. To do so, create `emms_therapy` and call `emmeans()`, placing `mod` in the "model" argument and the `Therapy` column in the "Specs" argument. Next, create `therapy_fx` by calling `contrast()`. Place our newly made `emms_therapy` in the "Object" argument and `therapy_contrasts` in the "Method" argument. Thus, `therapy_fx` will contain the results of a main effects analysis of Factor B (Therapy). Finally, create `stndrd_fx` which will contain a list of our main effects for factor A and B as well as their interactions.

```{r, factor_b_standard_analysis}
emms_therapy <- emmeans(mod, c("Therapy"))
therapy_fx <- contrast(emms_therapy, therapy_contrasts)
stndrd_fx = list(exp_fx, therapy_fx, interaction_fx)
```

Next, call `psyci()`, setting the following:

- The model is set as the previously made `mod` object, where the model must be made using the afex package (and of class afex_aov).

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made `all_fx` list.

- The method is set as "bf" to indicate a Bonferroni adjustment should be enacted.

- Alpha is set at .05.

```{r, get_cis}
output_ind <- psyci(
  model = mod, 
  contrast_tables = stndrd_fx, 
  method = "bf", 
  alpha = 0.05
) 

display_ind <- output_ind %>%
  unclass() %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(
    Experience = coalesce(contrast, Experience_custom),
    Therapy = coalesce(contrast, Therapy_custom),
  ) %>%
  select(estimate:psyr_p_value, Experience, Therapy) %>%
  relocate(Experience, Therapy)

display_ind[3, 1] <- NA
display_ind[4, 1] <- NA
display_ind[5, 1] <- NA
display_ind[1, 2] <- NA
display_ind[2, 2] <- NA


knitr::kable(display_ind, digits = 3)

```

## The Interpretation

Simple Effects Contrasts are of most use in helping understand what is driving an interaction effect. To demonstrate this, let's examine the interaction between **3yrs - \<1yr × Directive - Talking**, as well as its constituent simple effects contrasts.

This interaction looks at how the experience of a therapist (3 years versus less than 1 year) differentially impacts the outcomes of Therapy (the average of Directive versus Talking therapies). As a first port of call, it is helpful to return to our visualisation of the data, which intuitively shows that experience of a therapist seems to matter more for Talking therapies (Psychotherapy and Group) than for Directive therapies (Cognitive and Behavioural). By looking at the output from our main and interaction effects analysis, we can see that this effect is statistically significant, where the difference between years of experience leads to an increase on the DV (outcome of therapy) that is felt more by the average of Talking than the average of Directive therapies, where the difference between the two Factor B groups (Talking minus Directive) ranges from 12.196 to 25.804 points. This interpretation, while correct, is not especially useful. Specifically, it would be useful to quantify whether this effect is being differentially driven by either Directive or Talking therapies.

To understand what is driving the interaction, we may partition it into its two constituent simple effects contrasts: **3 yrs - \<1yr × Talking** and **3 yrs - \<1yr × Directive**. From these, and with reference to an a priori analysis, we learn the following:

- **3 yrs - \<1yr × Talking:** There is a statistically significant effect where therapists with 3 years of experience outperform those with less than 1yr of experience when administering either Group or Psychotherapy. Respectively, as compared to patients of therapists with less than 1 year of experience, patients of therapists with 3 years of experience have greater wellbeing scores on both Psychotherapy (8.94, 23.06) and on Group therapy (5.94, 20.06)

- **3 yrs - \<1yr × Directive:** There is insufficient evidence of a statistically significant effect. When administering Talking therapies, therapists with 3 years of experience may or may not outperform those with \< 1 year of experience, both in terms of Behavioural (-11.06, 3.06) and Cognitive (-12.06, 2.06)) therapies.

### The Benefits of CIs

By examining the CIs of each simple effects contrast, we can say the following: the A1B1 contrast **3yrs - \<1yr × Talking - Directive** is significant because the A1 effect (Years of Experience) is differentially felt at each level of B1, where 3 years of experience is only important when administering Talking therapies. Further, by examining the overlap (or lack thereof) between the simple effects confidence intervals, one can infer differences at the population level. For example, the CIs of the simple effects of Talking therapies at 3yrs- \< 1yr do not overlap with those of Directive therapies, implying that the population value for 3yrs- \< 1yr is different for Talking and Directive therapies. However, when comparing within Talking or Directive therapies, the simple effects CIs overlap, suggesting that at the population level these therapies lead to the same wellbeing impacts per level of therapist experience (3yrs - \< 1yr).

Finally, CIs allow a researcher to quantify the importance of an effect. Suppose that following new government guidelines, the researcher was only interested in an improvement in wellbeing of **at least 4 points**. If this were the case, while the main effect of Years of Experience is statistically significant, it may or may not be of importance, as the lower bound 2.122 is less than 4 units. On the other hand, the interaction of 3yrs - \<1 and Directive - Talking is both statistically significant and clinically important, as the lower bound -12.196 is more than 4 units.

### Limitations of a Simple Effects Analysis

Engaging in a simple effects analysis, as compared to an analysis of just main and interaction effects, comes at the cost of reduced power. This can be seen by comparing the outputs from our main and interaction effects analysis versus our simple effects analysis. Specifically. main effects and interaction effects - when analysed via an A Family simple effects model - have yielded less precise CIs. This reduction in power can be attributed to simple effects models necessarily having larger standard errors and critical constants per contrast. This is necessarily the case because we are looking at cell means; in a between subjects analysis simple effects contrasts will necessarily have a reduced $n$ as compared to a main and interaction effects analysis.
